summary.text: A nucleotide is a molecule made of a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate.
Nucleotides are the single units that link up to form the nucleic acid chains of DNA and RNA.
Beyond building DNA and RNA, nucleotides supply chemical energy in cells and take part in cell signaling.

facts.label: Three parts
facts.value: A nucleobase, a five-carbon sugar and a phosphate group

facts.label: Energy carriers
facts.value: ATP, GTP, CTP and UTP provide chemical energy

facts.label: Where they come from
facts.value: Obtained in the diet and made by the liver

facts.label: In food
facts.value: 5-nucleotides are additives that boost umami taste

items.prompt: A label calls a molecule a nucleoside triphosphate. What does that name tell you?

options.label: It contains three separate sugar rings
It carries three different nucleobases
Its phosphate group is made up of three phosphates
It is joined to three other nucleotides

items.explain: A nucleotide is called a mono-, di- or triphosphate depending on how many phosphates make up its phosphate group.

items.prompt: You remove the phosphate from a nucleotide. What is left?

options.label: The sugar and the nucleobase together, called a nucleoside
Only the nucleobase, because the sugar leaves too
Only the sugar, because bases are held separately
A short nucleic acid made of two sugars

items.explain: The sugar and nucleobase together are called a nucleoside.

items.prompt: A nucleotide in a cell has the sugar ribose. What is it called?

options.label: A deoxyribonucleotide
A nucleoside triphosphate only
A nucleobase
A ribonucleotide

items.explain: Nucleotides are termed ribonucleotides if the sugar is ribose and deoxyribonucleotides if it is deoxyribose.

items.prompt: In a double helix the two strands run in opposite directions. What does that allow?

options.label: Each strand to be built with no phosphate groups
Base pairing and complementarity between the strands
Nucleotides to swap sugars between the strands
The strands to hold completely different base sets

items.explain: The opposite orientation permits base pairing and complementarity, which is essential for copying and reading the encoded information.

items.prompt: Cells need chemical energy for many jobs. Which nucleotides supply it?

options.label: Nucleobases alone, with no sugar or phosphate
Cyclic nucleotides such as cAMP and cGMP
Nucleoside triphosphates such as ATP and GTP
Cofactor nucleotides such as coenzyme A

items.explain: ATP, GTP, CTP and UTP provide chemical energy, while cyclic nucleotides handle signaling.

items.prompt: Cells do not only take nucleotides from food. Which organ is the major site of making them from scratch?

options.label: The liver, working from common nutrients
The stomach, working from swallowed protein
The lungs, working from inhaled gases
The skin, working from sunlight alone

items.explain: The liver is the major organ of de novo synthesis, and nucleotides are made from common nutrients.

paragraphs.heading: What a nucleotide is
paragraphs.text: A nucleotide is an organic molecule with three parts: a nitrogen-containing base, a five-carbon sugar and a phosphate group. The sugar is either ribose or deoxyribose, and the phosphate group holds one to three phosphates. The sugar and base together, without the phosphate, are called a nucleoside. Nucleotides are the single building units, or monomers, of the two nucleic acids, DNA and RNA, which all life on Earth needs.

paragraphs.heading: The letters of DNA and RNA
paragraphs.text: DNA uses four bases: guanine, adenine, cytosine and thymine, shortened to G, A, C and T. RNA swaps in uracil, U, where DNA would use thymine. Adenine and guanine are purines; cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines. If the sugar is ribose, the unit is called a ribonucleotide, and if it is deoxyribose, a deoxyribonucleotide.

paragraphs.heading: Building a chain
paragraphs.text: In a nucleic acid, phosphates link the sugar of one nucleotide to the sugar of the next, over and over, making a long chain. These sugar and phosphate links form the backbone of a single or double helix. Each strand has a direction, running from its 5' end to its 3' end, named after carbon positions on the sugar. In a double helix the two strands point opposite ways, which lets the bases pair: adenine with thymine through two hydrogen bonds, and guanine with cytosine through three. That pairing is what makes copying and transcribing DNA's information possible.

paragraphs.heading: Energy, signals and helpers
paragraphs.text: Nucleotides do more than build DNA and RNA. Forms carrying three phosphates, such as ATP and GTP, supply chemical energy around the cell for jobs like making proteins and membranes, moving and dividing. Others, such as cyclic AMP and cyclic GMP, carry signals; in these cyclic forms one phosphate group is bound twice to the same sugar. Nucleotides are also built into cofactors, helper molecules for enzyme reactions, such as coenzyme A, FAD and NAD.

paragraphs.heading: Where they come from
paragraphs.text: We get nucleotides from food, and the liver also makes them from common nutrients. Making them from scratch, called de novo synthesis, draws on pieces from carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism, plus ammonia and carbon dioxide. The liver is the main organ for this. Cells can also recycle nucleotides through salvage pathways, breaking old ones down so their useful parts can go into new ones.

paragraphs.heading: Two routes for two shapes
paragraphs.text: Pyrimidines and purines are made by different pathways. For pyrimidines, the ring comes first, built from aspartate and carbamoyl-phosphate into a shared precursor called orotic acid, and only then is a phosphorylated sugar unit attached. Purines go the other way: their ring is assembled on top of the sugar. The purine route takes 10 steps to reach a branch point called IMP, and from there separate two-step routes lead to AMP and GMP. All of this happens in the cytoplasm, not inside any particular organelle.

paragraphs.heading: Outside the cell
paragraphs.text: In laboratory biochemistry, nucleotides can be made radioactive with radionuclides, giving radionucleotides. Some nucleotides are also added to food as flavour enhancers that boost umami taste, often in the form of yeast extract.
